content: I'm an intermediate at this. I understand that principal rays can locate an image, but how does the lens choose one image distance for all the other rays that leave the same object point?

The lens does not select a few privileged rays. Its curved surfaces give each incoming ray a direction change determined by the local surface normal and refractive index. For an ideal thin lens in the paraxial regime, those changes make every ray from one object point converge at the same corresponding image point. Principal rays are simply paths whose geometry makes that common point easy to find.
How does object distance alter that common meeting point? I know the focal length stays fixed, yet I sometimes picture the focus sliding backward when the object moves closer to the lens.

The focal point remains fixed; the image point moves. Light from a distant object point reaches the lens with little divergence, so the refracted rays meet near the focal plane. A nearby object sends a more divergent bundle into the lens. The lens supplies the same optical power, but the outgoing rays then converge less steeply and must travel farther before meeting.
When I cover half the lens, why does the whole image remain instead of losing its upper or lower half? It seems as though each lens region should own a matching image region.

Each small region of the lens receives rays from every visible object point, so each region contributes light to the entire image. Covering half removes some rays from every bundle rather than an entire bundle from selected object points. The full image therefore remains but becomes dimmer. Its sharpness may also change because the effective aperture and the mix of aberrated rays have changed.
How does that point-by-point rule produce an inverted image of an extended object? Is the crossing at the optical axis the cause, or just a convenient feature of the ray diagram?

For a real image, bundles from different object points cross in an ordered way. Rays from the top of the object converge below the axis, while rays from the bottom converge above it. The axis crossing is not merely diagrammatic; it expresses the geometry that reverses transverse position. Individual rays can cross elsewhere, but the mapping between object points and image points determines the inversion.

I'm an intermediate at this. When an object sits inside a converging lens's focal length, how does the lens form a virtual image if the refracted rays never physically collect at the projected location?

The refracted rays diverge, but their directions match rays that could have come from a larger object on the original side of the lens. Extending those paths backward makes them intersect at the virtual image point. No light collects there. The location is nevertheless precise because it describes the curvature, or vergence, of the outgoing wavefront and therefore how another optical system receives it.
How does the eye use that apparent location? I understand accommodation changes the eye lens, but I am not sure whether the retinal image is still real after starting from virtual rays.

The image on the retina is real. The magnifying lens sends a diverging bundle into the eye, and that bundle has the same vergence as light coming from the virtual image location. The eye accommodates for that incoming vergence, then its cornea and lens converge the rays onto the retina. Virtual describes the intermediate image, not the final retinal one.
When does moving the object toward the focal point make the virtual image larger? The thin-lens equation sends its distance outward, but I tend to treat that distance itself as the magnification.

As the object approaches the focal point from inside, the backward extensions intersect farther from the lens and the magnitude of the linear magnification increases. Image distance is not itself magnification; their connection is the ratio of image distance to object distance, with signs set by the chosen convention. Perceived enlargement also depends on angular size at the eye, so viewing position matters.
How could a second converging lens turn that virtual image into a real one? Does it focus the imaginary point directly, or only reshape the diverging bundle coming from the first lens?

It acts on the actual bundle, not on an imaginary object placed in space. For the second lens, the rays may behave as though they originate from a definite object point, so that point can be used in the lens equation. If the second lens gives the bundle enough convergence, the rays physically meet on its outgoing side and form a real image.
When would a screen fail even if I place it at the distance given for the virtual image? Is the problem simply that the screen is on the incident side of the lens?

The deeper issue is that actual rays do not converge at that location. A virtual image commonly lies on the incident side, but side alone is only a sign-convention clue. A screen records a sharp image only where each object point's real rays arrive together at a corresponding screen point. At the virtual location, only backward extensions meet, so no focused pattern exists to intercept.
I'm an intermediate at this. A biconvex lens has two refracting surfaces, so how do their separate bends combine into one focal power? I picture the refraction accumulating evenly through the glass.

Most of the direction change occurs at the two boundaries, not continuously through uniform glass. The first surface redirects a ray as it enters; the ray then travels straight inside until the second surface redirects it again on exit. Because the two surface normals have different orientations, both bends can steer a paraxial ray toward the axis. Their combined first-order effect is summarized as the lens's optical power.
How does the second surface keep from cancelling the first, since the ray changes from glass back to air? I know it bends away from the normal on exit.

Bending away from the normal does not necessarily mean bending away from the optical axis. On the second convex surface, the normal is tilted in the opposite geometric sense from the first interface. For the usual biconvex shape in air, the exit refraction generally adds to the inward deflection. Both index change and surface orientation determine the ray's final direction.
When is the thin-lens replacement by a single central plane accurate? Should thickness be compared mainly with the focal length, or with the object and image distances as well?

It is accurate when the separation of the surfaces produces negligible changes for the precision you need, usually with thickness small relative to focal length and curvature radii. Object and image distances matter because close conjugates can make a given positional error more significant. For a thick lens, you retain the same imaging logic but measure conjugate distances from two principal planes rather than one central plane.
How do marginal rays reveal the failure of that simple picture? They still refract at both surfaces, but their focal points seem spread along the axis rather than lying on one focal plane.

That spread is spherical aberration, which is distinct from thickness alone. The thin-lens formula assumes paraxial rays and small angles; marginal rays meet spherical surfaces at larger angles, where the approximations no longer hold. They commonly focus closer to the lens than near-axis rays. Thus even a geometrically thin spherical lens can lack one exact focus for a wide bundle.
When does an aspheric surface restore a single image point? Is it changing the lens power near the edge, or shifting the focal plane to average the remaining errors?

An aspheric profile changes surface slope with ray height so marginal rays receive a better-matched deflection. For one chosen conjugate pair and wavelength, a suitable profile can greatly reduce or ideally eliminate spherical aberration, bringing rays toward one image point. It is not merely averaging focal planes, although practical designs balance several residual aberrations across field angle, wavelength, and manufacturing constraints.
How does stopping down the aperture improve the image if it does not correct the surface itself? Does it just discard the rays whose convergence is least accurate?

Yes. A smaller stop blocks the outer rays, leaving a more paraxial bundle whose focal positions agree more closely. The lens has not changed, but the image spot shrinks because the strongest spherical aberration is excluded. The tradeoffs are less light and, at sufficiently small apertures, greater diffraction blur, so there is usually an aperture that gives the best overall sharpness.

I'm an intermediate at this. How does a glass lens form one image when its refractive index varies with wavelength? I associate chromatic aberration with colors arriving at slightly different focal times.

The separation is mainly spatial, not a difference in arrival time. Because refractive index depends on wavelength, the lens gives different colors different optical powers. In ordinary glass, blue light is usually bent more strongly than red light, so an uncorrected positive lens forms their best axial images at different distances. A white object therefore does not have one perfectly shared image plane.
When the sensor is placed between those color foci, how does the error appear around a small white point? Would one side look red and the other blue, or do the colors overlap symmetrically?

Near the optical axis, each wavelength produces a blur disk whose diameter depends on how far the sensor lies from that wavelength's focus. Those disks are centered at nearly the same location but have different sizes, producing colored halos rather than a simple red side and blue side. A directional color displacement is more characteristic of lateral chromatic aberration away from the axis.
How does lateral chromatic aberration differ in the image mapping? Is the magnification wavelength-dependent even when each color can be focused sharply somewhere near the same plane?

Yes. Lateral chromatic aberration means image scale varies with wavelength, so off-axis red, green, and blue image points land at slightly different transverse positions. Refocusing does little to remove that separation. Axial chromatic aberration instead assigns different best-focus distances to the colors and is most visible as defocus halos, including near the center of the field.
When does combining a positive crown-glass lens with a negative flint-glass lens help? The negative element seems as though it should undo both the color spread and some wanted convergence.

It does undo some convergence, so the positive element is made strong enough that the pair remains positive overall. The key is that crown and flint glasses have different dispersion relative to their refractive power. Designers choose curvatures and powers so two wavelengths share a focus while retaining the desired net focal length. Other wavelengths still leave a smaller secondary spectrum.
How can two selected wavelengths share a focus if every wavelength between them sees a different index? Does matching the endpoints automatically bring the middle colors close enough?

The power-versus-wavelength curves of the two glasses partly cancel when weighted by the element powers. Matching two wavelengths forces their net focal positions to coincide, and many intermediate wavelengths lie much closer to that common focus than with a singlet. They do not all coincide exactly because real dispersion curves are not scaled copies, which is why an achromat retains secondary color.
When would an apochromatic design be necessary rather than an achromat? Is the distinction only the number of color foci aligned, or does it also control spherical aberration across wavelengths?

An apochromatic design is useful when residual color from an achromat would limit resolution, as in demanding imaging across a broad spectral band. Conventionally it brings three wavelengths to a common focus and better controls the change of spherical aberration with wavelength, called spherochromatism. The label therefore describes more than simply adding another coincident color focus, though exact performance varies by design.
How does reducing the aperture hide axial color error? I assume the separate focal distances remain, so is the improvement just that each unfocused color cone becomes narrower?

Exactly. Stopping down does not make the wavelength-dependent focal distances coincide. It narrows the ray cones, so at a chosen image plane each defocused color forms a smaller blur disk. Color fringes become less conspicuous, although less light reaches the image and diffraction eventually grows. Optical correction changes the focal separation itself; aperture only reduces its visible consequence.

When using monochromatic light, does chromatic aberration disappear completely even though the lens still has dispersion? Would the remaining image errors then come only from geometry and diffraction?

With a truly single wavelength, chromatic aberration disappears because there are no different colors to separate, even though the material's dispersion still determines the index at that wavelength. Remaining limitations can include spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature, distortion, diffraction, scattering, and fabrication errors. Some of those affect sharpness, while distortion mainly changes where image points are mapped.
